newsitem.title: FINLAND: Light-weight steel beverage can challenges rivals.
newsitem.headline: Light-weight steel beverage can challenges rivals.

text.p: World steelmakers on Wednesday said they have developed a light-weight, tinplated steel to capture market share from aluminium and other beverage can materials.

Advances in tinplate production have led to a 20 percent reduction in steel can weight during the past 10 years, to 22 grammes for a 0.33 litre can, and steelmakers say that further "leightweighting" will ensure that the steel can is the packaging choice of the future.
An aluminium can weighs just over 11 grammes.
"We are going to drive this business," British Steel Executive Director John McDowall told Reuters at the International Iron and Steel Institute's (IISI) annual congress here.
"We are working with beverage and soft-drink manufacturers across Europe to get them interested," said McDowall, executive board member responsible for British Steel's tinplate business.
British Steel co-operates with European steelmakers Hoogovens, Rasselstein Hoesch and Sollac, to develop what they have dubbed the "Ultimate Can".

They presented the more than 300 IISI delegates with brightly-coloured conference-edition versions of a 22-gramme, 100 percent recyclable steel can, which the companies are using to push the concept with can-makers and can-fillers.

About 16 percent of the 160 billion metal beverage cans sold worldwide annually are made of steel, according to a presentation given at the IISI congress. But steel has captured 55 percent of the drink can market in Europe and its share has been rising.
In Japan, steel accounts for about 60 percent of the beverage can market, while in the United States steel beverage cans are hardly used at all.
"We have to encourage can-makers to make their investments," McDowall said, but he saw an even bigger hurdle in convincing beverage producers to adopt the steel can.
Steel-makers speak eagerly about the recyclability of steel, calling it the "world's most recyclable material". Aluminium cans are also 100 percent recyclable.
Prospects for growing steel consumption in the beverage packing business were also seen by Francis Mer, chairman of Europe's biggest steelmaker, Usinor Sacilor.
"We (in Europe) are way behind the U.S. in terms of beverage can consumption, so there is a lot of potential for growth," Mer told Reuters.
"You cannot say that the steel can will save European steel, but it is a growing market and it is our job to develop all parts of our business," Mer said.
Mer noted that levels of recycling vary greatly from one European country to the next, but he said the trend was generally increasing.

The steel beverage can has all but disappeared from the United States, where aluminum dominates the market, but some steelmakers say it is not entirely inconceivable that the steel can could make a come-back even there.
Curtis Barnette, chairman of Bethlehem Steel Corporation, said steel had a chance of getting back into the American beverage can market.
"I clearly see the opportunity, the interest and the ability for the steel can to become part of the beverage can industry -- even in the U.S.," Barnette said.
